summary.text: The pelagic zone is the water column of the open ocean, stretching from the sea surface down to the bottom, and it is split into regions by depth.
Going deeper, pressure rises while temperature and light fall, so the column can be divided into up to five layers, depending on how deep the water is.
Life thins out with depth: about 90% of marine life is packed into the sunlit top zone, the only one with enough light for photosynthesis.

facts.label: Number of layers
facts.value: Up to five, depending on water depth

items.prompt: A submersible sinks from the surface into deep open ocean. What happens to the water pressure and the light around it?

options.label: Pressure rises and light stays steady

items.explain: With depth, pressure increases while temperature and light decrease.

items.prompt: The sunlit surface zone is a thin slice of the whole ocean. Roughly what share of marine life is concentrated there?
items.explain: Nearly all primary production happens in the top zone, and about 90% of marine life lives there.

items.prompt: In a pitch-black deep zone that no sunlight reaches, what do most animals live on?

options.label: Seaweed growing on the deep floor
Minerals absorbed straight from the water
Dead matter drifting down from above
Plankton that thrives in the dark

items.explain: Most creatures there eat 'marine snow', detritus falling from the zones above, or prey on other animals at that depth.

items.prompt: Many animals in the dim layer just below the surface zone glow on their own. What is this glowing an adaptation to?
items.explain: The mesopelagic gets only a trace of sunlight, and many of its organisms evolved bioluminescence because of that.

items.prompt: A crab spends its whole life on the sediment at the very bottom of the sea. Which zone does it belong to?
items.explain: The benthic zone is the bottom region, including the sediment surface, and animals like clams and crabs living there are called benthos.

items.prompt: Some animals from the dim middle layers swim up to the surface waters only after dark. What do they come up to do?
items.explain: Some mesopelagic creatures rise to the epipelagic zone at night to feed.
